Title: Sub-Image Anomaly Detection with Deep Pyramid Correspondences
Authors: N. Cohen, Y. Hoshen
Plain-language summary: SPADE compares a new image with the most similar normal images it has seen, then checks every small region for a close match in those normal images. Regions that find no good match are marked as anomalous.
Research problem: Locate anomalies at sub-image (pixel) level using only normal training images.
Method: Two-stage k-nearest-neighbour (kNN) search: (1) retrieve the K most similar normal images using global ImageNet-pretrained features; (2) for every pixel, find the closest feature in a multi-scale feature pyramid of those K images; the distance is the anomaly score.
Architecture: Frozen ImageNet-pretrained ResNet (Wide-ResNet) feature pyramid; no training.
What it achieved: Reported a mean PRO of 91.7 on MVTec AD, well above the student and autoencoder baselines in the paper, with virtually no training time.
Limitations: Stores all normal features (memory grows with the dataset); kNN search is slow; no explicit handling of rotation; evaluated mainly in the full-data setting.
What to learn: The core reference-matching idea of this project: "is there a similar normal patch somewhere in the references?" It needs no defect labels.
Relation to this research: Direct ancestor of the proposed reference memory. The image-retrieval stage is similar to choosing the most relevant reference dies.
Unexplored: Few-shot behaviour with 1–10 references; semiconductor imagery; rotated targets.

Title: PaDiM: A Patch Distribution Modeling Framework for Anomaly Detection and Localization
Authors: T. Defard, A. Setkov, A. Loesch, R. Audigier
Plain-language summary: PaDiM learns, for every position in the image, what "normal" looks like as a statistical cloud of features. A new image is anomalous at a position if its feature lies far outside that cloud.
Research problem: Anomaly detection and localisation with a model that is cheaper than storing all normal features.
Method: For each patch position, fit a multivariate Gaussian (mean and covariance) to pretrained CNN embeddings from normal images; score with Mahalanobis distance.
Architecture: Frozen ResNet-18 or Wide-ResNet-50 features from several layers, randomly reduced in dimension.
What it achieved: Reported strong localisation on MVTec AD with low inference cost (see paper tables).
Limitations: Position-wise statistics assume the objects are aligned; covariance estimation needs many normal images per position, which is a poor fit for 1–5 references. The paper discusses a non-aligned test variant; check its section 4 before citing that result.
What to learn: If dies are well registered, position-specific statistics are a strong prior: a via should be at the same place in every die.
Relation to this research: Shows why alignment matters. Its per-position modelling becomes an option after geometric registration.

Title: Towards Total Recall in Industrial Anomaly Detection
Authors: K. Roth, L. Pemula, J. Zepeda, B. Schölkopf, T. Brox, P. Gehler
Plain-language summary: PatchCore keeps a compact "memory bank" of small normal image patches. For a new image, every patch looks up its closest normal patch; if even the closest one is far away, that patch is suspicious.
Research problem: Cold-start industrial anomaly detection with normal-only training data.
Method: Extract locally aggregated mid-level patch features; reduce the memory bank by greedy coreset subsampling; anomaly score = distance to the nearest memory feature; image score from the most anomalous patch.
Architecture: Frozen ImageNet-pretrained Wide-ResNet-50 (layers 2 and 3); no gradient training.
What it achieved: Up to 99.6% image-level AUROC on MVTec AD reported in the abstract, with strong localisation. The paper also reports a low-shot study.
Limitations: Scores are uncalibrated distances; features are pretrained on natural images; no orientation handling; memory grows with data before subsampling.
What to learn: The baseline for this project. Enrolment is 'add features to memory', not 'train a network'. That makes few-shot enrolment and feedback updates cheap and reversible.
Relation to this research: Proposed reference memory = PatchCore memory built from K reference dies, extended with alignment, open-set triage and verified updates.
Unexplored: Semiconductor imagery; controlled rotation; memory updates from feedback; unknown-vs-known separation.

Title: DRAEM – A Discriminatively Trained Reconstruction Embedding for Surface Anomaly Detection
Authors: V. Zavrtanik, M. Kristan, D. Skočaj
Plain-language summary: DRAEM paints fake defects onto normal images and trains a network to repair the image and point at the fake defects. After training, it can point at real defects it has never seen.
Research problem: Surface anomaly detection and segmentation without real defect labels.
Method: A reconstructive sub-network learns to remove synthetic anomalies; a discriminative sub-network segments anomalies from the original and reconstructed image together.
Architecture: Two U-Net-like encoder–decoders trained end-to-end on synthetic anomalies.
What it achieved: Reported strong pixel-level segmentation on MVTec AD (see paper tables).
Limitations: Needs many normal images to train; performance depends on how realistic the synthetic anomalies are; trained per category.
What to learn: Synthetic defect injection gives pixel-perfect masks for evaluation. This project uses it to test defect preservation under rotation.
Relation to this research: Not a few-shot method. Its synthetic-anomaly recipe is reused for the controlled benchmark (Section 17.7).
Unexplored: Few-shot training; SEM textures; rotated dies.

Title: Anomaly Detection via Reverse Distillation from One-Class Embedding
Authors: H. Deng, X. Li
Plain-language summary: A 'student' network learns to copy a 'teacher' network's description of normal images. On defects, the student fails to copy, and the disagreement shows where the defect is.
Research problem: Unsupervised anomaly detection and localisation.
Method: Teacher encoder (pretrained, frozen) → one-class bottleneck embedding → student decoder that reconstructs teacher features in reverse order; multi-scale feature discrepancy = anomaly map.
Architecture: Wide-ResNet-50 teacher; trainable bottleneck and decoder.
What it achieved: Reported state-of-the-art localisation on MVTec AD at publication (see paper tables).
Limitations: Requires training on many normal images per category; not designed for few-shot enrolment.
What to learn: Multi-scale feature discrepancy is an effective localiser. A useful full-data upper bound.
Relation to this research: Optional full-data baseline (upper bound) for experiments where many normal dies exist.

Title: FastFlow: Unsupervised Anomaly Detection and Localization via 2D Normalizing Flows
Authors: J. Yu, Y. Zheng, X. Wang, W. Li, Y. Wu, R. Zhao, L. Wu
Plain-language summary: FastFlow learns an exact 'probability of being normal' for each image location. Unusual locations get low probability.
Research problem: Density estimation of normal features for anomaly localisation.
Dataset: MVTec AD (further datasets in the paper; check the full text).
Method: 2D normalizing flow applied to pretrained feature maps; negative log-likelihood per location = anomaly map.
Architecture: ResNet / CaiT / DeiT backbones + trainable 2D flow blocks.
What it achieved: Reported 99.4% image-level AUC on MVTec AD (abstract), with efficient inference across backbones.
Limitations: Needs enough normal data to fit a density model; flow training can be unstable; not few-shot.
What to learn: A probabilistic score is easier to threshold than a raw distance, but only when enough data exists to fit it.
Relation to this research: Full-data comparison method; not a core component.

Title: EfficientAD: Accurate Visual Anomaly Detection at Millisecond-Level Latencies
Authors: K. Batzner, L. Heckler, R. König
Plain-language summary: EfficientAD is designed to be fast. A small student network learns to imitate a teacher on normal images, and an autoencoder checks global consistency.
Research problem: Accurate anomaly detection under strict latency limits.
Dataset: MVTec AD, VisA, MVTec LOCO AD.
Method: Patch description network (PDN) teacher distilled from a pretrained backbone; student–teacher discrepancy for local anomalies; autoencoder for logical/global anomalies.
Architecture: Lightweight 4-layer convolutional PDN; trained per category.
What it achieved: Reported about 2 ms latency and 600 images per second, evaluated on 32 datasets from three industrial anomaly-detection collections.
Limitations: Requires per-category training on many normal images; not few-shot.
What to learn: Latency matters for in-line inspection. Use it as a speed reference.
Relation to this research: Optional full-data, fast baseline for the inference-time comparison.

Title: Registration Based Few-Shot Anomaly Detection
Authors: C. Huang, H. Guan, A. Jiang, Y. Zhang, M. Spratling, Y.-F. Wang
Group: B. Few-shot and generalist anomaly detection
Plain-language summary: RegAD learns how to align images in general. Given a new product with only a few normal samples, it aligns the new image's features to those samples and flags parts that still do not match.
Research problem: Few-shot anomaly detection for new categories without retraining or fine-tuning.
Input modality: RGB images (MPDD: metal parts in varied positions).
Method: Train a category-agnostic feature-registration network (Siamese + spatial transformer modules) on many categories; at test time register test features to the K support images, estimate a normal distribution from the registered support features, and score deviations.
Architecture: ResNet-based Siamese network with feature-level spatial transformer networks (STN).
What it achieved: Reported AUROC gains over earlier few-shot methods of 5.1%, 6.9%, 8.0% (MVTec AD) and 3.2%, 5.0%, 3.4% (MPDD) for 2-, 4- and 8-shot settings (abstract).
Limitations: Registration is learned on natural-object categories; rotation is handled by augmentation and learned alignment, not evaluated as a controlled angle sweep; no semiconductor data; no unknown-vs-known separation.
What to learn: Alignment and few-shot detection should be solved together. A learned registration step can generalise to unseen categories.
Relation to this research: Closest work for Contribution 1 + 2. This project replaces learned feature registration with explicit, auditable die registration, and measures whether defects survive alignment.
Unexplored: Defect preservation under alignment; SEM / die imagery; same-wafer vs cross-wafer splits.

Title: Pushing the Limits of Fewshot Anomaly Detection in Industry Vision: GraphCore
Authors: G. Xie, J. Wang, J. Liu, F. Zheng, Y. Jin
Group: B. Few-shot and generalist anomaly detection
Plain-language summary: When an object is rotated, its patches look different to a normal CNN, so a few-shot memory needs more samples. GraphCore makes the patch description rotation-insensitive, so fewer samples cover more orientations.
Research problem: Few-shot anomaly detection when objects appear in different orientations.
Method: Visual isometric invariant features (VIIF) built with a graph representation of patch features; memory bank and nearest-neighbour scoring as in PatchCore. The paper also describes an 'Augmentation + PatchCore' baseline.
Architecture: Pretrained CNN features + graph neural network producing rotation-invariant patch features.
What it achieved: Reported average AUC increases of 5.8%, 4.1%, 3.4%, 1.6% (MVTec AD) and 25.5%, 22.0%, 16.9%, 14.1% (MPDD) for 1-, 2-, 4-, 8-shot cases (abstract).
Limitations: Rotation invariance can also hide defects whose meaning depends on orientation (for example, a line that should be horizontal). Evaluated on objects, not periodic die layouts.
What to learn: Rotation is a major cause of few-shot failure. Invariance and alignment are two competing solutions, and this project should compare both.
Relation to this research: Closest work for Contribution 2 (rotation). This project tests invariance against explicit alignment on die imagery, and checks for orientation-dependent defects.
Unexplored: Orientation-dependent defects; periodic semiconductor patterns; arbitrary-angle sweeps.

Title: WinCLIP: Zero-/Few-Shot Anomaly Classification and Segmentation
Authors: J. Jeong, Y. Zou, T. Kim, D. Zhang, A. Ravichandran, O. Dabeer
Group: B. Few-shot and generalist anomaly detection
Plain-language summary: WinCLIP uses a vision–language model (CLIP) and text prompts such as 'a photo of a damaged object' to find anomalies with zero or a few normal examples.
Research problem: Zero- and few-shot anomaly classification and segmentation.
Method: Compositional state prompts plus window-based CLIP features for zero-shot; WinCLIP+ adds few-shot normal reference matching.
Architecture: Frozen CLIP ViT image and text encoders.
What it achieved: Zero-shot 91.8% / 85.1% AUROC (classification / segmentation) on MVTec AD and 78.1% / 79.6% on VisA (abstract).
Limitations: Text prompts describe natural-object concepts. Semiconductor SEM vocabulary is outside CLIP's training data; coarse windows limit small-defect localisation.
What to learn: Language priors help zero-shot detection, but this project's references (normal dies) are more reliable than text for unseen die designs.
Relation to this research: Baseline for a 'no references' and few-shot comparison; SEM-CLIP adapts this idea to SEM data.

Title: Toward Generalist Anomaly Detection via In-context Residual Learning with Few-shot Sample Prompts
Authors: J. Zhu, G. Pang
Group: B. Few-shot and generalist anomaly detection
Plain-language summary: InCTRL is trained once and then used for new kinds of images. It compares a new image with a few normal examples and learns that 'large differences mean anomaly', whatever the image shows.
Research problem: One generalist anomaly detector that works on new datasets from a few normal samples without retraining.
Dataset: Nine datasets: industrial defects, medical images, semantic anomalies.
Method: In-context residual learning: residuals between query and few-shot normal prompts at patch and image level, combined with CLIP text priors, to train a generalist scorer.
Architecture: CLIP-based backbone with a residual learning head; trained on an auxiliary dataset.
What it achieved: Reported to significantly outperform competing methods across the nine datasets (see paper tables).
Limitations: Focuses on image-level detection scores; generalisation to SEM / die imagery not tested.
What to learn: Training on residuals (query minus reference) can transfer across domains. This matches the cross-wafer question.
Relation to this research: Strong candidate for cross-type generalisation (Experiment D) and an argument for residual-based scoring.

Title: ResAD: A Simple Framework for Class Generalizable Anomaly Detection
Authors: X. Yao et al.
Group: B. Few-shot and generalist anomaly detection
Plain-language summary: Instead of learning what each product looks like, ResAD learns what the difference between a sample and its closest normal reference looks like. The differences behave similarly across products.
Research problem: Anomaly detection on new classes without retraining.
Dataset: Industrial benchmarks incl. MVTec AD and VisA (see paper).
Method: Feature converter computes residual features relative to the nearest normal reference feature; a shallow constraint pulls normal residuals to a hypersphere; a distribution estimator flags out-of-distribution residuals.
Architecture: Pretrained backbone + feature converter + shallow constraintor + normalizing-flow-style estimator.
What it achieved: Reported strong cross-class generalisation (see paper tables).
Limitations: Number of normal references per new class must be checked in the paper; not evaluated on semiconductor data or rotation.
What to learn: Residual features are less class-specific than raw features. This idea fits cross-wafer and cross-type transfer.
Relation to this research: Candidate component for Contribution 1 (cross-die/cross-type transfer).

Title: AnomalyDINO: Boosting Patch-Based Few-Shot Anomaly Detection with DINOv2
Authors: S. Damm, M. Laszkiewicz, J. Lederer, A. Fischer
Group: B. Few-shot and generalist anomaly detection
Plain-language summary: AnomalyDINO is PatchCore-style nearest-neighbour matching, but with features from DINOv2, a self-supervised vision transformer. With even one normal image as reference, it finds anomalies very well on standard benchmarks.
Research problem: Training-free few-shot anomaly detection and segmentation.
Method: Patch-level deep nearest-neighbour matching on DINOv2 patch features; masking of background patches; image score from top anomalous patches.
Architecture: Frozen DINOv2 ViT (e.g. ViT-S/14); no training.
What it achieved: 1-shot image AUROC on MVTec AD increased from 93.1% to 96.6% (abstract).
Limitations: Natural-image pretrained features; ViT patch size (14 px) limits the smallest detectable defect unless images are upsampled; no rotation study; no semiconductor data.
What to learn: A strong, simple, training-free few-shot baseline. Exactly the 'give it a few samples, inspect new ones' setting.
Relation to this research: Closest work for Contribution 1. Primary baseline. This project adds die alignment, open-set triage and verified updates, and tests on semiconductor data.
Unexplored: SEM/die imagery; small defects vs patch size; rotation; same- vs cross-wafer.

Title: UniVAD: A Training-free Unified Model for Few-shot Visual Anomaly Detection
Authors: Z. Gu et al.
Group: B. Few-shot and generalist anomaly detection
Plain-language summary: UniVAD first splits an image into its parts (components), then compares each part with the matching part of a few normal images. It also checks whether the parts relate to each other correctly.
Research problem: One training-free few-shot detector across industrial, logical and medical domains.
Dataset: Nine datasets incl. MVTec AD, VisA, MVTec LOCO, Brain MRI, Liver CT.
Method: Contextual component clustering (with vision foundation models), component-aware patch matching for structural anomalies, graph-based component aggregation for logical anomalies.
Architecture: Frozen foundation models (segmentation + feature encoders); no training on the target domain.
What it achieved: Reported state-of-the-art few-shot performance across domains (see paper tables).
Limitations: Heavy foundation-model pipeline; component segmentation may not transfer to dense periodic SEM layouts; no rotation study.
What to learn: Component-aware matching restricts comparison to the 'same kind of part'. This is close to region-aware matching in die layouts.
Relation to this research: Baseline for few-shot detection; idea for region-restricted matching.

Title: Unsupervised Continual Anomaly Detection with Contrastively-learned Prompt
Authors: J. Liu et al.
Group: C. Continual learning, feedback and open-set
Plain-language summary: UCAD learns new product types one after another without forgetting the old ones, by storing small 'prompts' and a key–knowledge memory for each task.
Research problem: Task-agnostic continual learning for unsupervised anomaly detection and segmentation.
Method: Continual prompting module with key–prompt–knowledge memory; structure-based contrastive learning using SAM.
Architecture: Frozen ViT backbone + learnable prompts + SAM-guided contrastive learning.
What it achieved: Reported improvements of 15.6% (detection) and 26.6% (segmentation) over previous continual AD methods (arXiv abstract).
Limitations: No human verification of what is learned; tasks are product categories, not drifting inspection streams; not semiconductor.
What to learn: Memory-based continual learning can avoid catastrophic forgetting without retraining the backbone.
Relation to this research: Shows continual AD is feasible. This project's feedback loop is simpler (memory edits) and adds human verification.
Unexplored: Human-verified updates; noisy feedback; semiconductor drift.

Title: Training-Free Human-in-the-Loop Anomaly Detection via Memory Bank Correction
Authors: A. Abbas, S. Abbas, K. Adhikari
Group: C. Continual learning, feedback and open-set
Plain-language summary: An expert corrects a PatchCore detector's mistakes by editing its memory of normal patches. No retraining. When the detector raises a false alarm, normal patches from that image are added to memory, but only if they are genuinely new.
Research problem: Correcting a memory-bank anomaly detector with expert feedback, without retraining or original training data.
Method: Start from a bank of 10 normal 'golden' samples; for false positives, add patches through a self-calibrating novelty gate (only patches beyond the median pool-normal nearest-neighbour distance); held-out evaluation with 20 splits per category and Holm-corrected Wilcoxon tests. Feedback simulated from ground truth.
Architecture: PatchCore (frozen backbone + memory bank) with memory editing operations.
What it achieved: Corrections recovered a median 66% of the gap to a fully trained bank and improved 12 of 15 MVTec AD categories without harming any (abstract). Passive and active querying were statistically indistinguishable; a defect-memory extension failed.
Limitations: Preprint; simulated, noise-free feedback; natural-object data; no rotation; no unknown-defect triage.
What to learn: Crucial evidence and a warning: adding corrected images to memory inflates naive evaluation through memorisation. A held-out protocol is mandatory.
Relation to this research: Closest work for Contribution 5. This project extends it to semiconductor dies, noisy/incorrect feedback, quarantine and rollback, and known/unknown defect memories.
Unexplored: Noisy or adversarial feedback; reference contamination; semiconductor data; defect memory that works.

Title: An Evaluation of Continual Learning for Advanced Node Semiconductor Defect Inspection
Authors: A. Prasad, B. Dey, V. Blanco, S. Halder
Group: C. Continual learning, feedback and open-set
Plain-language summary: When a defect detector is taught new defect types from a new process step, it tends to forget old types. This paper measures how well continual-learning methods prevent that on real fab SEM images.
Research problem: Incremental learning of new SEM defect classes across process steps (ADI → AEI) without forgetting.
Dataset: Resist-wafer SEM images at After-Development Inspection (ADI) and After-Etch Inspection (AEI); not public.
Method: Task-incremental continual learning benchmark against conventional fine-tuning.
Architecture: Supervised defect detection network (see paper).
What it achieved: Reported better results than conventional supervised training and showed that plain fine-tuning quickly forgets earlier defect classes.
Limitations: Proprietary data; supervised detection needs box labels; no few-shot normal-reference setting.
What to learn: Forgetting is real on semiconductor data. Feedback updates must be checked for forgetting, not only for gains.
Relation to this research: Motivates the forgetting-rate metric and replay-based safeguards in Stage 10.

Title: An Unknown Wafer Surface Defect Detection Approach Based on Incremental Learning for Reliability Analysis
Authors: Z. Zhao, J. Wang, Q. Tao, A. Li, Y. Chen
Group: C. Continual learning, feedback and open-set
Plain-language summary: A wafer-defect model that keeps learning online as new, previously unknown defect types appear, while protecting what it learned before.
Research problem: Online detection of unknown wafer defects with incremental learning.
Dataset: Wafer defect data (dataset name not confirmed in this session; check the paper).
Method: PIRB: restricts updates of important weights to retain old knowledge and keeps a tiny reference buffer of previously seen defect patterns.
Architecture: Deep classifier with weight-importance regularisation + replay buffer.
What it achieved: Reported 60% shorter training time than offline learning and 10% higher total accuracy than compared methods (abstract).
Limitations: Classifier-based; no pixel localisation reported in the abstract; dataset details unverified here.
What to learn: A small replay buffer plus weight protection is a practical anti-forgetting recipe.
Relation to this research: Supports the 'small verified buffer' design of the feedback stage.

Title: Catching Both Gray and Black Swans: Open-set Supervised Anomaly Detection
Authors: C. Ding, G. Pang, C. Shen
Group: C. Continual learning, feedback and open-set
Plain-language summary: DRA uses a few labelled defect examples to learn 'seen' anomalies, but keeps a separate path to catch completely new anomalies so they are not ignored.
Research problem: Using a few labelled anomalies without overfitting to them, while still detecting unseen anomaly types.
Dataset: Nine real-world datasets incl. MVTec AD, AITEX, SDD, ELPV, Mastcam, BrainMRI, HeadCT, Hyper-Kvasir.
Method: Disentangled representations for seen anomalies, pseudo (augmented) anomalies and latent residual anomalies.
Architecture: CNN backbone with multiple heads.
What it achieved: Reported better detection of both seen and unseen anomalies than prior methods (see paper tables).
Limitations: Image-level focus; needs some labelled anomalies; not semiconductor.
What to learn: Few known defects should help, not narrow, detection. Keep a 'deviation from normal' path that is independent of known classes.
Relation to this research: Design rule for Stage 8: known-defect memory is added next to, not instead of, the normal-reference score.

Title: Scanning Electron Microscopy-Based Automatic Defect Inspection for Semiconductor Manufacturing: A Systematic Review
Authors: E. Dehaerne, B. Dey, V. Blanco, J. Davis
Plain-language summary: A careful survey of 103 papers on automatically finding defects in SEM images of chips. It explains which approaches were popular and what is still hard.
Research problem: Systematic review of automatic SEM defect inspection algorithms.
Method: Systematic literature review (database search, screening, taxonomy).
What it achieved: Reports that reference-based defect detection was the most common algorithm type until 2020, after which deep learning became dominant, especially for classification.
Limitations: Review; does not benchmark methods; literature cut-off before 2025 developments.
What to learn: Reference-based comparison is the historical backbone of SEM inspection. A learned reference memory is a natural evolution, not a break.
Relation to this research: Positions the project: it connects the classical reference paradigm with modern few-shot deep features.

Title: Defect Detection in Patterned Wafers Using Anisotropic Kernels
Authors: M. Zontak, I. Cohen
Plain-language summary: Instead of perfectly aligning a die image to a reference die, this method tries to rebuild the inspected image from pieces of the reference. Whatever cannot be rebuilt is a defect.
Research problem: Defect detection in patterned wafers without explicit registration.
Method: Anisotropic-kernel reconstruction of the inspected image from a reference image; unreconstructable regions flagged.
Architecture: Classical non-parametric reconstruction; no learning.
What it achieved: Demonstrated registration-free reference-based detection on patterned wafers.
Limitations: Assumes the reference is defect-free; single reference; hand-designed.
What to learn: Classical precedent for 'compare with a reference, without pixel-perfect alignment'. Patch matching with a search window does the same in feature space.
Relation to this research: Historical anchor for the alignment-tolerant matching design (Stage 5).

Title: Automatic Defect Segmentation by Unsupervised Anomaly Learning
Authors: N. Ofir, R. Yacobi, O. Granoviter, B. Levant, O. Shtalrid
Plain-language summary: An industry team trains a segmentation network on clean SEM backgrounds with pasted-in fake defects, so it learns to find defects in a single SEM image without needing a reference image.
Research problem: SEM defect segmentation without manual labels and without a reference image.
Method: U-Net-style network trained on automatically generated samples: clean backgrounds with copy-paste 'defect implants', plus contrastive-style feature losses.
Architecture: U-Net-style encoder–decoder.
What it achieved: Demonstrated label-free defect segmentation from the defect image alone.
Limitations: Proprietary data; synthetic-implant realism; no few-shot reference enrolment.
What to learn: Industry already uses reference-free and implant-based training. Synthetic implants are a valid evaluation tool if reported honestly.
Relation to this research: Supports the synthetic defect-injection benchmark; offers a reference-free comparison point.

Title: SEM-CLIP: Precise Few-Shot Learning for Nanoscale Defect Detection in Scanning Electron Microscope Image
Authors: Q. Jin, Y. Jiang, X. Lu, Y. Liu, Y. Chen, D. Gao, Q. Sun, C. Zhuo
Plain-language summary: SEM-CLIP adapts a vision–language model to SEM images of chips, so it can classify and outline nanoscale defects after seeing only a few examples.
Research problem: Few-shot defect classification and segmentation in SEM images.
Method: CLIP adapted with SEM-specific prompts and mechanisms that focus on defect regions and suppress background.
Architecture: CLIP ViT encoders + adaptation modules.
What it achieved: Reported to surpass PromptAD in the 10-shot setting on the in-house dataset.
Limitations: Private data; no public reproduction; rotation and unknown defects not addressed.
What to learn: Few-shot learning on real SEM defects is feasible, and domain adaptation of foundation models matters.
Relation to this research: Closest semiconductor few-shot work; a comparison point if a public implementation exists.
Unexplored: Public benchmark; normal-reference memory; open-set; feedback.

Title: Unsupervised Integrated-Circuit Defect Segmentation via Image-Intrinsic Normality
Authors: B. Zhao, Q. Shi, S. Lyu, Y. Lu
Plain-language summary: Because chip layouts change between products and are hard to align, this method stops comparing with external reference images. It finds what is normal inside the test image itself (repeated structures) and segments what does not fit.
Research problem: Unsupervised IC defect segmentation without external normal references.
Method: Learnable normal-information extractor aggregates representative normal features from the test image; a coherence loss ties them to normal regions; defects segmented as non-coherent regions.
Architecture: Deep encoder with a normal-feature extractor head.
What it achieved: Reported effective segmentation on IC data (numbers not retrieved in this session).
Limitations: Preprint; relies on repetition within each image; may fail when a defect repeats or a structure is unique within the field of view.
What to learn: An important counter-argument: external-reference matching is brittle for IC images when layouts vary and alignment is hard. The proposal must test this risk directly.
Relation to this research: Closest semiconductor competitor to the reference-guided idea. A combined score (external reference + intrinsic normality) is a natural extension.
Unexplored: Combining intrinsic and reference cues; feedback; wafer context.

Title: Image-Intrinsic Priors for Integrated Circuit Defect Detection and Novel Class Discovery via Self-Supervised Learning
Authors: B. Zhao, X. Wang, S. Lyu, Y. Lu
Plain-language summary: Extends the previous paper: it finds defects without a support set and also groups new defect types that nobody has named yet.
Research problem: Support-set-free IC defect detection plus novel class discovery (NCD) of unseen defect types.
Dataset: Real-world IC SEM dataset (paper describes several fabrication stages; details not verified here).
Method: Image-intrinsic priors for detection; self-supervised classifier with IC defect priors; semi-supervised k-means to estimate the number of unknown classes.
Architecture: Self-supervised encoder + clustering head.
What it achieved: Reported validation on a real-world IC dataset (numbers not retrieved in this session).
Limitations: Preprint; private data; NCD needs a batch of unknown samples to cluster.
What to learn: 'Unknown defect' handling can go further than flagging: unknowns can be clustered into candidate new classes for engineer review.
Relation to this research: Informs Stage 8 (unknown triage) and the engineer workflow 'mark for investigation'.
Unexplored: Reference-guided NCD; human verification of discovered classes.

Title: Domain Adaptation for Image Classification of Defects in Semiconductor Manufacturing
Authors: A. Poniatowski, N. Gentner, M. Barusco, D. Dalle Pezze, S. Salti, G. A. Susto
Plain-language summary: A defect classifier trained on SEM images from one setting often fails in another. This Infineon / university study tests domain-adaptation methods that adapt the classifier with few or no labels from the new setting.
Research problem: Cross-domain SEM defect classification (source → target domain shift).
Dataset: SEM defect images (see paper for exact datasets).
Method: Semi-supervised (SSDA) and unsupervised (UDA) domain adaptation methods applied to SEM defect classification.
Architecture: CNN classifiers with domain-adaptation objectives.
What it achieved: Reported as the first application of SSDA/UDA to this kind of semiconductor image classification (authors' claim).
Limitations: Classification only; closed set; no localisation.
What to learn: Cross-domain shift is real in semiconductor SEM data. Cross-wafer and cross-type inspection cannot be assumed to work.
Relation to this research: Evidence for treating cross-wafer generalisation (Contribution 1, scenario 2) as a hypothesis to test.
Unexplored: Normal-reference memories under domain shift; localisation.

Title: LogicQA: Logical Anomaly Detection with Vision Language Model Generated Questions
Authors: Y. Kwon, D. Moon, Y. Oh, H. Yoon
Plain-language summary: A vision–language model writes a checklist of questions about what a normal image should look like, then answers them for each new image. Wrong answers point to logical anomalies, and the answers explain the decision in words.
Research problem: Training-free, few-shot logical anomaly detection with explanations.
Dataset: MVTec LOCO AD; proprietary semiconductor SEM dataset.
Method: VLM-generated question checklist from few normal images; answers aggregated into anomaly scores and explanations.
Architecture: Large vision–language model (prompting only).
What it achieved: Reported 87.6% AUROC and 87.0% F1-max for logical anomalies on MVTec LOCO AD; SEM results described as strong without public numbers.
Limitations: Logical (global) anomalies, not pixel localisation; proprietary SEM data; VLM cost.
What to learn: Explanations help engineers verify decisions, which is relevant to the feedback interface.
Relation to this research: Possible extension for engineer-facing explanations; not a core component.

Title: Advancing SEM Based Nano-Scale Defect Analysis in Semiconductor Manufacturing for Advanced IC Nodes
Authors: B. Dey, M. Monden, V. Blanco, S. Halder, S. De Gendt
Plain-language summary: A pipeline that classifies, boxes and outlines nanoscale defects in SEM images. To avoid drawing pixel masks by hand, it learns masks from bounding boxes only.
Research problem: Unified classification, detection and segmentation of SEM defects with cheap (box-level) labels.
Method: Deformable DETR detection feeds BoxSnake box-supervised instance segmentation.
Architecture: Deformable DETR + BoxSnake.
What it achieved: Demonstrated pixel-precise masks from box supervision on ADI SEM data (see paper for numbers).
Limitations: Supervised; closed set; private data.
What to learn: Pixel masks are expensive in fabs. Box-level annotation is a realistic compromise, and evaluation must match the annotation level.
Relation to this research: Informs the annotation strategy (Stage 7) and the supervised upper-bound baseline.

Paper: Dolgener Cantú et al. (InP golden die)
Title: Deep Learning-based Multi Project InP Wafer Simulation for Unsupervised Surface Defect Detection
Authors: E. Dolgener Cantú, R. K. Wittmann, O. Abdeen, P. Wagner, W. Samek, M. Baier, S. Lapuschkin
Plain-language summary: For small-volume InP wafers there are too few identical dies to compare against. This work generates a realistic 'golden die' image from the CAD design and compares the real die with it.
Research problem: Reference-based defect detection when few repeated dies exist (multi-project wafers).
Dataset: InP multi-project wafer images with CAD layouts (see paper).
Method: Deep network trained to render photo-realistic wafer images from CAD; pixel-wise comparison of simulated and real images.
Architecture: Image-to-image generative network (see paper).
What it achieved: Demonstrated simulated golden references for unsupervised detection (numbers not retrieved here).
Limitations: Preprint; needs CAD data; simulation errors become false alarms.
What to learn: When repeated dies are scarce, the reference can be synthesised. This is a fallback for cross-type inspection with very few samples.
Relation to this research: Alternative reference source for Contribution 1; relevant to cross-type experiments.
Unexplored: Combination with few real references; rotation.

Title: Automated Detection and Classification of Defective and Abnormal Dies in Wafer Images
Authors: H.-C. Chen
Plain-language summary: From a picture of a whole wafer, the method finds each die's row and column, builds a wafer map, and classifies defective and abnormal dies.
Research problem: Die extraction and indexing from whole-wafer images, then defective-die classification.
Method: Clustering to estimate die rows and columns (instead of template matching), wafer-map construction, CNN classification.
Architecture: Clustering + CNN classifier.
What it achieved: Reported good identification of defective-die patterns and a wafer map for diagnosis.
Limitations: Die-level classification, no pixel localisation; single imaging modality.
What to learn: Die extraction and indexing (row, column) is the bridge between die images and wafer maps.
Relation to this research: Informs Stage 1 (die extraction) and Stage 9 (wafer-level indexing).
Unexplored: Few-shot anomaly detection inside each die.

Title: Exploring Active Learning for Semiconductor Defect Segmentation
Authors: L. Cai, R. S. Pahwa, X. Xu, J. Wang, R. Chang, L. Zhang, C.-S. Foo
Plain-language summary: Instead of asking an expert to label everything, the model picks the images it would learn most from. This reduces annotation effort for semiconductor defect segmentation.
Research problem: Reduce annotation cost for semiconductor defect segmentation.
Dataset: X-ray microscopy scans of semiconductor samples (see paper).
Method: Active learning sample selection for segmentation, addressing domain shift and class imbalance.
Architecture: Segmentation network + acquisition function.
What it achieved: Reported reduced annotation effort; identified domain shift and class imbalance as the main obstacles.
Limitations: X-ray, not SEM/optical; supervised segmentation.
What to learn: Engineer time is the scarce resource, so feedback requests should be prioritised.
Relation to this research: Supports an active-query option in the feedback loop.

Title: Wafer Map Failure Pattern Recognition and Similarity Ranking for Large-Scale Data Sets
Authors: M.-J. Wu, J.-S. R. Jang, J.-L. Chen
Plain-language summary: This paper introduced WM-811K, a very large collection of wafer maps: pictures that show which dies on a wafer passed or failed. It also classifies the spatial failure patterns such as 'edge ring' or 'scratch'.
Research problem: Recognise and retrieve wafer-level failure patterns at scale.
Dataset: WM-811K: 811,457 wafer maps; 172,950 labelled into 9 classes (incl. 'none').
Input modality: Wafer maps (die pass/fail grids), not images of die surfaces.
Method: Radon-transform and geometry features; SVM classification; similarity ranking.
Architecture: Hand-crafted features + SVM.
What it achieved: Released the dataset that became the standard wafer-map benchmark.
Limitations: No die-surface appearance; no pixel masks; label imbalance (most labelled maps are 'none').
What to learn: Wafer-level spatial patterns are a different problem from die-surface defects. Do not mix the two.
Relation to this research: Data source for the optional wafer-level context study (Stage 9, Contribution 4) only.
Unexplored: Linking die-image anomalies to wafer-map patterns.

Title: Few-Shot Classification of Wafer Bin Maps Using Transfer Learning and Ensemble Learning
Authors: H. Kim, H. Yoon, H. Kim
Plain-language summary: To recognise a new wafer-map failure pattern from only a few examples, the model is first trained on simulated wafer maps and then fine-tuned on the few real ones.
Research problem: Few-shot classification of wafer bin maps.
Dataset: Simulated wafer bin maps for pre-training; a real WBM dataset for evaluation (see paper).
Method: Pre-train on simulated maps; fine-tune several classification heads (ensemble) on few real maps.
Architecture: CNN with ensemble of classification layers.
What it achieved: Reported to outperform meta-learning methods commonly used for few-shot WBM classification on a real dataset.
Limitations: Wafer-map level; closed set.
What to learn: Simulation-based pre-training is a practical answer to label scarcity in fabs.
Relation to this research: Supports synthetic pre-training and the few-shot wafer-level extension.

Title: Enhanced Detection of Unknown Defect Patterns on Wafer Bin Maps Based on an Open-Set Recognition Approach
Authors: J.-S. Shin, M.-J. Kim, B.-S. Kim, D.-H. Lee
Plain-language summary: In fabs, engineers usually spot new wafer-map patterns by experience. This method automatically flags maps whose pattern does not belong to any known class.
Research problem: Detect unknown defect patterns on wafer bin maps.
Dataset: Wafer bin maps incl. new patterns from real manufacturing (see paper).
Method: Open-set recognition with constrained mean filtering and Radon-transform features; one-class SVM.
Architecture: Feature extraction + one-class SVM.
What it achieved: Reported over 98% detection performance for various defect classes on new patterns from real manufacturing.
Limitations: Wafer-map level; no die-image localisation.
What to learn: Open-set recognition works at wafer level. The same idea is needed inside each die image.
Relation to this research: Evidence for Stage 8 design at wafer level; motivates die-level open-set triage.
